"This is what true innovation looks like. From its 3.5L EcoBoost® technology to its ultra-efficient aerodynamics, the Ford GT is the culmination of everything great we do at Ford. ...everything about the Ford GT is designed to deliver pure performance." - Ford Motor Company.

Based on Eric Broadley's Lola GT, the original Ford GT40 was spawned by the Dearborn giant's ambition to beat Ferrari at Le Mans, a feat it duly achieved for the first time in 1966. The GT40 project had commenced three years previously, following Ford's failed attempt to buy into Ferrari, and was based at the Ford Advanced Vehicles plant at Slough, England. The GT40 first ran competitively in 1964 but failed at Le Mans that year and again in 1965. That first sweet Le Mans victory would fall to the 7.0-litre Mark II, with victory the following year going to a US-built Mark IV 'J' car. (The GT40 Mark III was the British-built road-going version). Of the three GT40s that lined up together for that famous 1-2-3 clean-sweep finish at Le Mans in 1966, the first two were entered by Shelby American while the third, driven by Ronnie Bucknam and Dick Hutcherson, was entered by Holman & Moody.

A decade later and the GT40's status as an all-time great classic sports car had been firmly established, leading to an increased demand for unmolested originals and the start of a replica-building industry. Perhaps the only surprise concerning the emergence of a reconstituted 'official' version is that it took Ford the best part of 40 years to get around to it.

The 'new generation' GT was developed by Ford's Special Vehicle Team Engineering department under the direction of John Coletti and Fred Goodnow. The composite body panels were unstressed, as on the original, but instead of the monocoque chassis construction used in the 1960s, SVT Engineering developed an all-new aluminium spaceframe combining extruded sections and panels. Doubling as fuel reservoirs, a pair of massive sills contributed much to the original's chassis stiffness, whereas the new GT relied on a centre-tunnel 'backbone' that greatly improved ease of entry and exit. The suspension design was an advance on the original's, consisting of unequal-length control arms and a pushrod/bell-crank system acting on horizontally mounted coil spring/damper units. Braking was handled by six-piston, Alcon callipers with cross-drilled and ventilated discs all round.

In defeating Ferrari's more highly stressed V12s, Ford proved that the traditional American V8 possessed all that was necessary to compete at the cutting edge of international endurance racing. A far cry from the simple pushrod units of the 1960s, the supercharged MOD 5.4-litre V8 produced 550bhp at 5,250rpm and 500lb/ft of torque at 3,250 revs; figures on a par with those of the 7.0-litre engine that won at Le Mans in 1966 and 1967. The all-synchromesh six-speed transaxle used ZF internals and was sourced from RBT Transmissions, whose founder Roy Butfoy had been a member of Ford's racing team at Le Mans. The interior featured leather-upholstered, Recaro bucket seats with aluminium ventilation grommets embedded into the panels. The instrument layout followed the original's, comprising analogue gauges and a large tachometer complemented by modern versions of the traditional toggle switches.

Back in 1966, the Ford GT40 endurance racer became the first car to exceed 200mph along the Mulsanne straight at Le Mans. Matching that would be some achievement for the production road car, even allowing for nearly 40 years of technological progress. Tested for Motor Trend magazine by Indycar racing legend Bryan Herta, the new Ford GT duly topped 200mph at Ford's Kingman test facility in Arizona, emphatically demonstrating that it was indeed worthy of that famous name. A total of 4,038 cars had been completed when production ceased at the end of 2006, over three quarters of which were delivered in the USA.

In 2015 a third-generation Ford GT was unveiled at the North American International Auto Show. Technologically a far cry from its predecessors, the new Ford GT featured a 3.5-litre twin-turbocharged V6 engine; a carbon-fibre monocoque chassis; carbon-fibre body panels; pushrod suspension; and active aerodynamics. Producing 647bhp, the EcoBoost turbo V6 drove the rear wheels via a Getrag seven-speed DCT gearbox. The factory claims a sub-3.0 second 0-60mph time and a top speed of 216mph (347km/h), which makes the Brembo carbon-ceramic brakes a necessity rather than a luxury.

In fact, Ford's new supercar had been created with GT racing in mind, hence the presence of an integral roll cage and a host of other competition-car technologies. Yet despite its start-of-the-art track-focused suspension, the GT has a ride quality rivalling that of a luxury saloon. Autocar's Matt Prior was obviously impressed: "the GT... has a level of composure - that balance between ride and handling – that I'm not sure I've better experienced in 20 years of road testing. It's so compliant, yet there's so little roll, and body movements are so well controlled, that is genuinely astonishing". All of the planned 1,000 road models had been sold before deliveries commenced in 2017, and these exclusive supercars remain highly sought after today.
And as for its maker's racing aspirations, the new GT did not disappoint. At Le Mans on 19th June 2016, the number '68' Ford GT of Ford Chip Ganassi Racing driven by Hand/Müller/Bourdais finished 1st in the LM GTE-Pro class, their victory marking 50 years after Ford's first Le Mans win in 1966 with the original GT40.

In 2018 Ford announced a new limited edition model: the Carbon Series, which was positioned in the range midway between the regular GT and the Competition Series. As its name suggests, the Carbon Series made much more extensive use of this lightweight material than the GT, while the adoption of a titanium exhaust and carbon-fibre wheels helped reduce the weight by 18kg. Air conditioning and an infotainment system were retained (unlike in the US-only Competition Series) while other notable special features included anodised paddle shifters and silver stitching on the seats and steering wheel. The GT's engine was retained unchanged.

Ford updated the GT for the 2020 model year, introducing several mechanical upgrades and new special editions. The 3.5-litre blown V6 now incorporated gallery-cooled pistons, higher-energy ignition coils and larger intercoolers, and produced 651bhp while at the same time delivering a 'broader torque band' according to Ford, although peak torque remained unaltered. Previously optional, the standard exhaust was now the lighter titanium system by Akrapovič, which still delivered the GT's evocative engine note. The suspension was now stiffer in Track mode, and the rear buttresses had been redesigned to increase airflow over the car. Production of the second-generation GT ceased in 2022.

This Ford GT Carbon Series, "GT N166", left the factory on 13 September 2022 and was delivered in France to its first and current owner. Finished in silver grey, complemented by exposed carbon fibre stripes, it features red Brembo brake calipers and exposed carbon fibre door mirrors. In keeping with the Carbon Series specification, it is equipped with a titanium exhaust system, as well as gloss carbon fibre wheels secured by titanium wheel nuts. The interior also makes extensive use of carbon fibre, while the steering wheel is trimmed in Alcantara with stitching matching the GT's exterior colour.

Preserved in its owner's private collection since delivery, this extremely rare GT Carbon Series has covered only 23 kilometres at the time of cataloguing.

Offered with its service booklets still factory sealed, its tool kit, battery maintainer and original car cover, it has furthermore been registered in France since 2025, with all taxes paid, and therefore comes with a French registration document. It is also supplied with its spare set of keys, along with its production file, including factory build sheets and manufacturing photographs.

Representing what is likely one of the last examples of its kind, the Ford GT is a pure, non-hybrid hypercar. This example, virtually new yet already registered, is therefore ready to be enjoyed both on the road and on the track.

Although best remembered as a 1960s style icon favoured by the fashion-conscious 'Mods', the Lambretta motor scooter - together with Piaggio's rival Vespa - had been intended as basic transport for the non-enthusiast masses. Manufactured by the Italian industrial giant Innocenti, the Lambretta gained instant acceptance in the immediate post-war years, its cleanliness and convenience in particular appealing to those who regarded the true motorcycle with suspicion. Introduced in 1947, the first Lambretta 'A' employed an open frame with pressed-steel front section and tubular rear, in which sat a 125cc two-stroke engine, setting the pattern for all Lambrettas to follow. By the end of 1950 Innocenti was producing up to 100 per day. Predecessor of the Li and TV series, the LD arrived in 125cc form in 1951 and became available with a 150cc engine three years later. The LD 125's engine produced 4.8bhp, giving the model a top speed of around 45mph (72/km/h). LD production continued until the end of the 1950s.

This charming Lambretta and sidecar combination was purchased by the vendor from a large private collection in Germany, whose owner sold it due to its advancing years. The combination presents well and comes with Italian registration documents. If you are planning a Roman holiday, here is your ideal transport!

Announced at the 1968 Geneva Salon, the Mercedes-Benz 300 SEL 6.3 was the ultimate wolf in sheep's clothing. Visually, the car was practically identical to other W109 models, but - thanks to the 600 limousine's fuel-injected 6,332cc V8 - offered stupendous performance. Air suspension, a limited-slip differential, and four-wheel disc brakes came as standard. One of only 6,526 produced, the example offered here was first delivered in California in June 1970. Finished in Silver Grey Metallic with black leather interior, this magnificent Mercedes-Benz is in beautifully preserved condition, having travelled only 15,000 kilometres since restoration. Gabriel Voisin was perhaps France's greatest aviation pioneer. In 1907 he built the first practical aeroplane capable of leaving the ground under its own power, and his Avions Voisin company was the first mass producer of aircraft in the world. The end of WWI in 1918 brought a halt to Voisin's aviation ventures and forced him to look elsewhere to provide employment for his workforce. The result was some of the most original and innovative automobile engineering of the inter-war era, especially in the field of passenger-car aerodynamics, as exemplified by this C30.

In 1937, following the restructuring of Voisin, the company's new owner commissioned the production of a new model: the C30. Continental Motors' 3.6-litre six-cylinder Graham engine was chosen for the C30 and could be ordered with a supercharger, which boosted maximum power from 90 to 116bhp. The outbreak of WW2 put a stop to the C30's brief production run (around 20 or 30 were made, only five of which are known to survive) and they are historically significant as the last Voisin automobiles.

This C30 was first registered on 27th June 1939 as '7405 RM 6', then a Parisian number. It was subsequently registered as '8673 DR 75' to one Emile Janet, residing at 4, rue Clement Marot in Paris, on 24th March 1955. There is a plaque on the dashboard saying 'René Janet, 16, rue Franklin, Paris', which was mistakenly thought to refer to the coachbuilder (it may refer to an owner of the car, maybe linked to Emile Janet?); however, the car's actual coachbuilder is still unknown. Mr Strinati imported the Voisin from France into Switzerland in October 1963.

In December 1984, the car was treated to some restoration work: the body was repainted in BMW Savanna Beige, the headlining redone, the radiator shell repaired, the chrome re-plated, and the Plexiglas windows in the roof replaced. Some black and white photographs of the C30 (still wearing its French Parisian registration plates) taken by Mr Strinati show it in a darker colour. We believe that the car was originally painted dark green, as upon close inspection traces of dark green paint were found in various places. Apart from the aforementioned changes the car remains highly original.

More recently, the Voisin, together with other cars belonging to Mr Strinati's collection, was exhibited in the 'Musée Jean Tua de l'Automobile' in Geneva. Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, Carrozzeria Ghia enjoyed a fruitful relationship with the Chrysler Corporation. The result was some of the most spectacular styling exercises and concept cars ever seen, which were the sensations of the era's motor shows.

Chrysler's products of the late 1940s were typically well engineered but somewhat dated in appearance, although that would change in 1949 with the arrival from Studebaker of master stylist Virgil Exner. Exner rejuvenated Chrysler's line up and collaborated with Ghia to create to create some of the era's most memorable styling exercises, commencing with the XX-500 of 1951. This large coupé was styled by Exner and manufactured by Ghia, though later concept cars would be designed and built entirely in Italy.

Taking its name from C B Thomas – head of Chrysler's export division – the 'Thomas Special' was based on the Exner-designed, Ghia-built Styling Special but on the longer standard wheelbase, making it a full five-seater. Thomas used it as his personal car. Virtually identical apart from a different front grille, the GS1 variant was shown at the Paris Motor Show in 1953, and Ghia would go on to build a limited run (18-19) of similar cars.

Little else is known of this Thomas Special until 1982 when it featured in an article by Denis Adler published in Car Collector magazine's December edition: "the sports coupe is possible (sic) the original Thomas Special although there is no documentation." According to historian Raphael Burnett, the car was in Switzerland, as evidenced by photographs showing a Swiss sticker on the front bumper.

Eventually the Thomas Special was sold to restorer Fran Roxas, and in the 1980s was restored by him for the second time, such was his commitment to perfection; indeed, the Thomas Special was considered one of the finest restorations in his collection. In 1992 the Thomas Special was sold to the Bortz Auto Collection, home to some of the most spectacular concept/dream cars of the 1950s and 1960s. The interior was restored by Chris Nersthiemer and the car exhibited at the Pebble Beach Concours d'Elegance that same year. In 1997 the Thomas Special was one of 27 cars from the Bortz Auto Collection featured in the Chicago Tribune.

The Thomas Special was meticulously cared for and used sparingly, and by the time it was sold at a US auction circa 2007 had covered a mere 1,000-or-so miles while in Mr Bortz's custodianship. In 2010 the car was exhibited at Meadow Brook and on 1st April 2016 was registered in the UK. It has been registered in Romania since 2020/2021.

Combining the best of American styling and Italian coachwork, the Thomas Special is worthy of a place in any important private collection.

"Delage have to their credit many world's records, including a world's championship, and more awards at the principal Concours d'Élégance than any other car in the world... To these achievements Delage have added a third and greater. They have made the highest known degree of luxury and performance available at the price the average motorist can pay."

Delage's publicity had every right to sing the praises of what - arguably - was the finest French car of its day and the only one that could be mentioned in the same breath as the 32CV Hispano-Suiza in terms of elegance and engineering excellence. Founded in 1905 by Louis Delage, the company commenced production with a single-cylinder De Dion-engined runabout and within a few years was offering multi-cylinder designs. The publicity value of racing was recognised right from the start, a single-cylinder Delage winning the Coupe Des Voiturettes as early as 1908 and Louis himself taking the 1911 Coupe de l'Auto in a 3-litre four-cylinder. Victories at the Grand Prix du Mans and the Indianapolis 500-Mile Race were achieved prior to WWI, the company going on to become a major force in Grand Prix racing in the 1920s and setting a new World Land Speed Record mark in 1924 with a 10.7-litre overhead-valve V12.

Four- and six-cylinder D-series cars formed the mainstay of the company's touring car production in the 1920s, and then at the 1929 Paris Salon Delage launched the Maurice Gaultier-designed D8. A magnificent 4.0-litre overhead-valve straight-eight featuring an X-braced chassis and servo-assisted Perrot-type brakes, the D8 was destined to attract the creative attentions of Europe's finest coachbuilders. The impressive list of discerning D8 owners includes King Gustav V of Sweden, King Alexander of Yugoslavia, and Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia as well as leading businessmen, politicians, and film stars of the day. The Autocar magazine said this of the D8: "...all the speed that can possibly wanted, and extremely rapid acceleration are obtained with practically no noise at all, and driven normally the car is docile..."

Along with many other manufacturers of quality cars, Delage was badly affected by the economic downturn of the early 1930s. Despite the favourable reception for its new range, Automobiles Delage went into receivership in April 1935 and shortly thereafter was taken over by Delahaye. The Delahaye takeover spelled the end for the original D8. From then onwards, Delages were built to Delahaye designs but retained their own superior short-stroke engines and hydraulic brakes.

The post-war years were difficult times for makers of large and luxurious automobiles in France. Taxation rates were punitive for cars of over 2 litres, choking off demand, and in 1950 the combined total production of Delahaye and Delage was only 235 units. This unsustainable situation worsened over the next two years and in 1953 Delage production stopped. It was a sad end to a once great marque.

Representing the ultimate expression of the eight-cylinder Delage, this supremely elegant D8-120 was ordered in December 1938 by the Swiss Delage and Delahaye representative Albert Goy of Garage du Kursaal in Geneva for their customer, Mr Gossweiler of Bern. Delahaye commissioned the cabriolet body from the celebrated Parisian coachbuilder Henri Chapron, who completed the work the following summer.

The car comes with copies of the factory records stating that it was ordered in black with a red interior and a black alpaca hood, while a thin red coachline was applied to the body. The Delage was specifically ordered with Securit glass; two indicators at the front and at the rear; two extra fog lights; an extra powerful horn; and a steering column-mounted ignition key doubling as an anti-theft device. The client also specifically requested that the rear seats should be removable and that the rear floor was to be flat so he could store bulky luggage such as hunting gear (Chapron refused to comply with that last request blaming the shape of the chassis as an excuse).

There is a wealth of correspondence with all parties mentioned above, most interestingly a very detailed letter from Mr Gossweiler complaining about the poor build quality of the bodywork, most notably the fixing of the dashboard and the hood cover (which he had remade). Mr Gossweiler considered keeping the amount he was due to pay upon collecting the car as a guarantee for the work that was to be carried out on it!

This car has always stayed in Switzerland and was later owned - in 1949 - by the Industrialist Ludwig Zweifel of Glaris (CH) and then by dentist Walter Meier domiciled in Blonay (in the Vaud canton) from 1953. Pierre Strinati bought the Delage circa 1960/1961 from Carrosserie Graber, who fully repainted the car and retrimmed the hood in April 1961 (bill on file). The paintwork was changed to two-tone dark grey over black (probably during Mr Strinati's ownership), which suits the D8 very well. The leather interior remains original, as does the rest of the car.

More recently the Delage was pictured in Henry Rasmussen's book The Survivors. A copy of the latter is on file and the car also comes with old Swiss registration papers. Recommissioning will be required following a lengthy period of inactivity. Close inspection recommended.

In 1959 Mercedes-Benz debuted four new models at the Frankfurt Show - the 220 SEb (W111) among them. Two-door Coupé and Convertible models appeared in 1960 and 1961 respectively, minus the already dated-looking tail fins of the saloon. More modern in style, the luxurious, hand-built 220 SEb Coupé and Convertible were better appointed too, being equipped as standard with a rev counter, leather upholstery and four-speed automatic transmission. Front disc brakes were fitted from the start of production. These top-of-the-range two-door models simply oozed quality in every department, and it is not surprising that they quickly became favourites among celebrities, royalty and industrialists, often seen in the most glamorous destinations worldwide.

Delivered new in Singen, Germany, this beautiful Mercedes-Benz 220 SEb Convertible has the rare four-speed manual transmission and matching numbers (chassis and engine). Carefully preserved and well maintained throughout its lifetime, the car has had two or possibly three owners in Germany plus one in the Netherlands. According to our vendor, the car has covered only 108,550 kilometres and is still highly original and in good condition. It is finished in the timelessly beautiful colour combination of Dunkelgrün (dark green) with a gorgeous brown leather interior and a brown convertible top. The body looks magnificent and has clearly been well cared for; it has been resprayed only once (for cosmetic reasons) and still looks good. The convertible top is easy to operate and fits nicely, and the car sits on its original steel wheels. Beautifully patinated, the interior seems completely original and appears just as well cared for as the rest of the car, while the seats are as comfortable as one would expect in a top-of-the-range Mercedes.

The car is powered by the 2.2-litre version of Mercedes-Benz's dependable M127 inline six producing 120bhp (DIN). Perfectly complemented by the four-speed manual transmission, the engine is said to be wonderfully smooth and to run beautifully. The chassis and brakes are also very well suited to their task and contribute to the comfortable driving experience; indeed, its relaxed road manners make the 220 SEb Convertible ideal for top-down, cross-country touring.

The car underwent extensive maintenance in 2022 and was serviced in 2023, 2024, and 2025. Well documented, it comes with the original data card; original Fahrzeugbrief; and its original wallet and all books (including the stamped service booklet). It currently has a Dutch registration. It is exceedingly rare to find an unrestored and unmolested Mercedes-Benz 220 SEb in such great condition as this one.

"Introduced in 1937, the Mercedes-Benz 320 was a comfortable car available in a huge range of bodywork configurations, from a four-door saloon costing 8,950 marks, via a six-seater touring car, a number of cabriolets and a roadster, up to a streamlined saloon available for 14,550 marks." - Schlegelmilch & Lehbrink, Mercedes.

Mercedes-Benz's luxurious 320 series was introduced in 1937 as a replacement for the 290 series. Built initially in two wheelbase lengths - regular and short (N) - the 320 was down to just one from 1938 onwards, though a wide variety of open and closed body styles remained available, including a state-of-the-art streamlined saloon. The 320's six-cylinder side valve engine started out at 3,208cc before being bored out to 3,405cc towards the end of production to compensate for inferior quality fuel. Maximum power increased to 78bhp and overall performance greatly improved, while coil-sprung independent suspension all round ensured that the ride afforded the ultimate in comfort at all times. Mercedes-Benz made only a little over 4,300 320s in all body styles, so this 320N Cabriolet is both rare and collectible.

Benefiting from the larger, 3.4-litre engine, chassis number '408250' is probably one of only six 320N cabriolets completed. Unfortunately, all purchase order books were destroyed during WW2, which means that there is no official data available concerning chassis and engine numbers. Research, and the files with the car, suggest that this could be one of the original six built at the Mannheim factory.

Restored in 2002 by the renowned restorer Szielasko from Switzerland, this 320N comes complete with tool kit, a set of suitcases, and a history file containing numerous photographs of the rebuild. The car is ready to be enjoyed!

"When it was first announced by Mercedes-Benz, the production 300 SL Coupé was a startling car built to the German concern's customarily startling standards, but above all what left the general public most open-mouthed about the new car was its upward-opening Gullwing doors...!" - Motors, 1963.Post-war, Mercedes-Benz had returned to competition in 1952, fielding two of its new 300 SL (W194) sports cars in the Mille Miglia. The pair finishing a creditable 2nd and 4th overall in this most difficult of events, and this promising start was followed up by a win in the challenging Carrera Panamericana. The works first raced the 300 SL (Sport Leicht) in open form, but for the Le Mans 24-Hour Race in June a trio of 'gullwing'-doored coupés was entered. High sills were a feature of the multi-tubular spaceframe chassis, and while access was not a problem of the open car, the enclosed coupé bodywork required innovative thinking - hence the gullwing doors. Karl Kling and Hans Klenk duly brought their 'Silver Arrow' home in 1st place at Le Mans and the 300 SL was on its way to becoming part of motor sporting legend.

Launched in 1954, the production 300 SL road car retained the spaceframe chassis and lightweight aluminium-alloy bodywork of the W194 racer, while its mechanical underpinnings, like the latter's, owed much to the contemporary Mercedes-Benz 300 luxury saloon. A 2,996cc overhead-camshaft inline six, the 300 SL's engine was canted over at 45 degrees to achieve a low bonnet line and produced 215bhp (DIN) at 5,800rpm using Bosch mechanical fuel injection. A four-speed, all-synchromesh manual gearbox transmitted power to the hypoid bevel rear axle. Suspension was independent all round: by wishbones and coil springs at the front, with swing axles and coil springs at the rear.

A production 300 SL (W198) was tested by Road & Track magazine in 1955, accelerating from 0-60mph in 7.4 seconds on its way to a top speed of 140mph (225km/h). Half expecting the long-awaited 300 SL to provide an anti-climax, R&T were delighted to find the new car, "far beyond our wildest expectations. In fact, we can state unequivocally that in our opinion the 300 SL coupé is the ultimate in an all-round sportscar. It combines more desirable features in one streamlined package than we ever imagined or hoped would be possible. Performance? It accelerates from a dead start to 100mph in just over 17 seconds. Dual purpose? A production model 300 SL can make a very acceptable showing in any type of sportscar competition. Yet the car is extremely tractable and easy to drive in traffic. Comfort? The fully enclosed 300 SL is the most comfortable (and safe) high-speed 'cross-country' car built today".

A 300 SL roadster featuring conventional doors was first exhibited at the Geneva Salon in May 1957 and, although built in greater numbers, has never matched the immortal Gullwing for desirability. Its racing parentage notwithstanding, the 300 SL remains a thoroughly practical car, as civilised in city traffic as it is exhilarating on the Autostrada. By the time 300 SL Gullwing Coupé production ceased in 1957, some 1,400 examples had found customers. Today the model is both rare and most sought after by connoisseurs of fine automobiles.

This magnificent Mercedes-Benz 300 SL Gullwing is a desirable matching numbers example, retaining its original chassis, body and engine. Recorded in Eric Le Moine's 300 SL Register, this car left the factory on 9th August 1955 and was delivered new on 25th August 1955 in New York City via Mercedes-Benz Distributors, Inc. Originally finished in Silver Gray Mettalic with blue leatherette and tartan cloth upholstery, the car has been repainted in black and the interior retrimmed in red leather. It is worth noting that this car is equipped with a very rare option on the 300 SL: a long axle ratio (1 : 3.42) allowing it to exceed 260 km/h, which explains the speedometer graduation up to 180 mp/h. This option was chosen by the first owner when ordering the car. In general, 300 SL Gullwing have a gear ratio of 1 : 3.64 and a speedometer graduated only up to 160mph

The Gullwing enjoyed four owners in the USA before coming to the UK in 1980 where it was extensively restored towards the end of that decade. The car belonged to two owners in the UK before passing to the French vendor, a Parisian collector, in 2011. The current owner sent the car to MB Classic at Stains for a full overhaul, which included having the injection pump rebuilt; new injectors fitted; all hoses replaced; brakes completely rebuilt; water and oil radiators rebuilt; starter motor rebuilt; alternator rebuilt; general vehicle inspection, etc, etc. There are related invoices totalling in excess of €60,000 on file. The car has been serviced regularly by MB Classic at Stains and GFB Classic-Auto.

During a recent test drive we have noted that the engine started immediately and ran smoothly, revving without difficulties, performing well at low and high speeds, shifting gears smoothly and with brakes working correctly.

Also on file is an Expertise valuation report noting that the car is in "excellent overall running order" and "visible parts of the underbody and chassis are in very good condition, with no visible signs of accident damage or rust going through the metal". A fine example of one of the 20th Century's most coveted classics, this beautiful Mercedes-Benz 300 SL Gullwing comes complete with fitted luggage; sundry invoices for maintenance and repairs; the aforementioned Expertise report; a valid French Carte Grise; and an up-to-date Contrôle Technique.

YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1956 DESCRIPTION:
• One of only 843 XK140 fixed-head coupés made with right-hand drive
• Delivered new to Switzerland
• Strinati family ownership from new
• Believed genuine 3,150 kilometres from new
• Requires recommissioning

Launched in 1954, the Jaguar XK140 was broadly similar to, though more refined than, its sensational XK120 predecessor, major engineering changes being confined to the repositioning of the engine 3" further forward and the adoption of rack-and-pinion steering as used on the racing C-Type. The suspension and brakes remained much as before, though with stiffer torsion bars at the front and telescopic shock absorbers at the rear, replacing the previous lever type. As before, three models were offered: roadster, coupé and drophead coupé, the latter two offering usefully increased cabin space and occasional rear seats. Outwardly the newcomer was distinguishable by its revised radiator grille, rear lights incorporating flashing indicators, and larger bumpers.

The power unit remained Jaguar's well-tried, 3.4-litre, twin-cam six, which now produced 190bhp in standard trim. A close-ratio gearbox enabled better use to be made of the increased performance, while Laycock-de Normanville overdrive became an option for the first time.

An original right-hand drive model, this XK140 coupé was despatched from the factory on 6th March 1956 to Jaguar agent Garage Claparède in Geneva, Switzerland, and on 6th April 1959 was sold by them to Madame Jeane Strinati, Pierre Strinati's mother, who is listed on the accompanying JDHT Certificate as first owner. The aforementioned heritage certificate records the original colour scheme as Cream with red interior, but Claparède's invoice states that the car was Grey (the colour it is today). A note written by Mr Strinati himself mentions that the car was Cream when imported (as attested by the swiss customs documents), so it must have been repainted upon its arrival in Geneva.

The odometer reading is 3,150 kilometres, which could very well be the distance covered from new given the car's remarkable state of preservation the car appears to have its fully original interior and exhaust manifold coating). Close inspection is recommended.

The car comes with instruction manuals; a wealth of Jaguar Drivers' Club correspondence (Mr Strinati was a life member having owned several examples including, among others, an SS100, an XK150S and an E-Type, the last two bought new. As with all the other cars in the collection, the Jaguar has been stored on axle stands for many years and will require recommissioning.

YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1971 DESCRIPTION:
• One of only 425 Ghibli SS 4.9 coupés built
• Delivered new in Italy
• Desirable manual transmission example
• Enthusiast ownership for 20 years (2004-2024)
• Well maintained

Unveiled at the 1966 Turin Auto Show, the Maserati Ghibli quickly distinguished itself as a formidable competitor in the Gran Turismo marketplace, standing alongside legends such as the Ferrari 365 GTB/4 'Daytona' and Lamborghini Miura. It was this competitive landscape that drove Maserati to introduce the Ghibli SS. The original Ghibli was equipped with a 4.7-litre V8 engine that produced around 306 horsepower. The Ghibli SS, however, came with a 4.9-litre V8 producing around 335bhp; its top speed of 280km/h (174mph) made it - at the time - the fastest Maserati road car ever produced.

Designed by Giorgetto Giugiaro at Carrozzeria Ghia, the Ghibli is celebrated for its striking looks, featuring a long hood, sleek lines and a low, elongated silhouette. This blend of elegance and aggressiveness typifies Italian sports cars of the 1960s and '70s. Beyond its thrilling performance, the Ghibli SS offers a refined level of accommodation for two passengers and their luggage, affording the perfect combination of luxury and speed. With around 425 examples produced, the Ghibli SS coupé is a rare and highly sought-after classic.

This Maserati Ghibli SS, chassis number 'AM115/49 1948', was manufactured on 25th November 1970. Delivered new in Italy, it was finished in elegant Oro Longchamps with a black leather interior, and is equipped with the 4.9-litre SS engine and the ZF five-speed manual transmission.

Acquired in 2004 by its previous (French) owners (members of the Club Maserati France), the Ghibli has been meticulously maintained over the past 20-or-so years. Accompanying documentation on file reveals a history of careful stewardship, including detailed service records from Landrin Sport et Collection in the Ardennes (2006-2016); Pierre Nallet's Garage du Trident in 2009; and Trident, a Maserati specialist in the Vendée in 2017. A 2016 expert appraisal on file confirms the car's outstanding condition, noting its nice paintwork, perfectly aligned bumpers, and original dashboard. There are also technical inspections from 2010, 2012 and 2017, and a French Carte Grise. Additionally, a repaint and major service were completed at the Ateliers des Légendes for €17,000, ensuring that this Ghibli SS not only looks stunning but is also thoroughly prepared and a delightful driving experience. More recently, the retractable headlights were overhauled and the battery replaced, and the car passed a French Contrôle Technique (technical inspection) in September 2024.

description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1934 DESCRIPTION:
Engine block serial no. 102401.59
Vanvooren body no. 2933

• One-off, matching numbers
• One of only 18 W29 coupés built
• One of only a handful of W29 built with French coachwork
• Delivered new to Paris, France
• Present ownership since 1959
• Formerly on display in the Musée de l'Automobile Jean Tua, Geneva
• Outstandingly original

Sensation of the 1934 Berlin Auto Show, Mercedes-Benz's legendary pre-war 500K supercar cost a small fortune when new and today commands a king's ransom, such is its rarity. The 1930s decade was a period of unprecedented fertility in motor car styling, of which the sublime 500K represented the very pinnacle of excellence. Its timeless appeal endures to this day (the original name of the model, 'Typ 500 mit Kompressor', was later shortened to '500K').

Beneath its seemingly endless bonnet, the 500K's eight-cylinder engine developed 100bhp un-supercharged or 160bhp with the compressor engaged. The car had a top speed approaching 110mph (177km/h). After testing a 500K cabriolet in 1936, The Autocar declared: "This is a master car, for the very few. The sheer insolence of its great power affords an experience on its own."

The Mercedes-Benz 500K and its successor, the 540K, are among the most iconic models of the classic era. A total of 761 chassis of the two W29 models—the 500K and 540K—were produced at the Stuttgart-Untertürkheim plant between February 1934 and November 1939: 342 with a 5-litre engine and 419 with a 5.4-litre engine. Of these, 691 units were fitted with bodies by the "Sonderwagenbau" department at the Sindelfingen plant, while only 70 chassis were delivered to external coachbuilders for bodywork. The most popular model was the Cabriolet B, with 296 units produced, while the exclusive and dignified Special Roadster achieved a total production run of around 50 units. The various coupé variants amounted to only 12 cars, and just 6 examples of the Autobahn Kurier were built.

The chassis of the 500K and 540K had a wheelbase of 3,290 mm and was available in two versions. In addition to the standard configuration, there was a variant in which the radiator, engine-gearbox unit, steering gear and seats were moved rearwards by just over 10 cm. Roadsters, Special Roadsters, Cabriolet A and Autobahn Kurier models were built on this rearward-engine chassis, while all other body variants were constructed on the standard chassis.

According to Mercedes-Benz Classic in Stuttgart, the delivery of chassis no. U105.394 to the Paris branch was recorded in the commission book on 29 November 1934, shortly after the model's first presentation at the Paris Salon in October. Unfortunately, there is no mention of either the customer or the coachbuilder. (According to a letter from DaimlerChrysler Schweiz AG dated 27 November 2006, this car—chassis number "U105394"—was delivered new to Germany; this information has since been proven to be incorrect.)

The number 102401.59 stamped on the engine block provides the following information:
10 for the Untertürkheim plant
24 for the new M24 engine type
01 for the series
59 for the 59th engine of the first series

This corresponds with the total production of 105 units in 1934 and, together with the original engine plate no. U105.394, confirms that this car is matching numbers.

Although sales opportunities for Mercedes-Benz on the French market were limited by exorbitant import duties of 45%, the company maintained a showroom on the Champs-Élysées and regularly exhibited its latest models at the Paris Salon in October. Internal documents from the Mercedes-Benz board of directors show that attendance at the Salon was considered a "must" in order to present the brand to international customers. One way to partially circumvent import duties was to deliver bare chassis—a strategy that proved successful, as the 500K/540K chassis attracted the interest of the most prestigious coachbuilders of the time.

This particular example features a fixed-head coupé body by Vanvooren, one of the most renowned and successful French luxury-car coachbuilders of the 1930s. Carrosserie Vanvooren, based in Courbevoie in north-west Paris, bodied the majority of Hispano-Suiza chassis during this period and also designed and built numerous bodies for Bugatti, Delage, Rolls-Royce, Bentley, Packard and Cadillac. These automotive gems are among the most exclusive one-off creations and can be found today in the world's most prestigious collections.
As confirmed during a thorough inspection by Vanvooren specialist Martin Waltz in December 2025, the Vanvooren body number 2933 appears in several locations on the vehicle and dates from August 1938. What happened to the chassis during the three years following its delivery from Stuttgart to Paris remains unknown. It is possible that it remained unsold during this period, but it may also have received an initial body that was later replaced in 1938. Among the Parisian elite of the 1930s, it was common practice either to purchase new cars at short intervals or to have existing ones modernised. There are countless examples of this trend, often driven by the regularly held Concours d'Élégance, which demanded the very best. Alternatively, it may simply have been a matter of a new owner with new tastes.

As was customary, Vanvooren prepared a design proposal for the customer, illustrated in Jan Melin and Sven Hernström's book Mercedes-Benz 8: The Supercharged 8-Cylinder Cars of the 1930s, Volume 2 (copies of the relevant pages on file). In addition to the spectacular front wings and the rearward-mounted engine/radiator unit, the use of a design feature introduced two years earlier by the coachbuilder Letourneur & Marchand is particularly striking: the pillarless, overlapping front and rear side windows with a rearward-sloping line. Vanvooren employed this feature on several other bodies as well. It is not known with certainty whether the car's first paintwork was dark green, as it is today; however, there is much to suggest this was the case, as the largely original all-green interior—with leather-covered dashboard and window surrounds—corresponds perfectly with Vanvooren's preference for single-colour paintwork and interiors.

It can be assumed that the Mercedes remained in France until 1947, when it first appeared in Geneva, Switzerland. That year, the Vanvooren-bodied Mercedes caught the attention of 18-year-old schoolboy Pierre Strinati. Carrying Swiss dealer plates "GE 2325," it was parked on the curb in front of Garage Verolet at 107 Boulevard de la Cluse (see pictures). Immediately fascinated, Strinati found the courage to enquire about the extraordinary vehicle, despite not yet having a driving licence. The green car was offered for sale at CHF 3,500. He photographed it and cherished the images from that moment on, never expecting to see the Mercedes again (handwritten notes and photographs by Mr Strinati are on file).

The 500K was photographed once more, this time in front of the Eaux-Vives Garage owned by Blanc & Paiches, now without a number plate (the photographer is unknown). Together with Strinati's images, these are the earliest known photographs of the car. Official importation from France to Switzerland followed the next year, as evidenced by the customs clearance certificate dated 31 July 1948 (document on file).
Eleven years later, during a visit to Montreux on the opposite side of Lake Geneva, Pierre Strinati was unexpectedly reacquainted with his dream car. Now painted black, it was driving slowly through town. He ran after it and, when it stopped in front of the "Le Pavillon" tea house, approached the driver, Kaspar Schmid—who was also the proprietor of the establishment. When Strinati asked whether he might consider selling the car, Schmid replied in the affirmative, much to his surprise. Thus, on 29 January 1959—67 years ago to the day—the Mercedes changed hands for the final time, for CHF 10,000.

This Mercedes became the first car in what would grow into one of the most remarkable private collections in the world. Strinati, the only son of a wealthy textile manufacturer, had been cultivating his passion for automotive design since the mid-1950s and, by the mid-1960s, had assembled in his private garage nearly every marque now considered a blue-chip classic. The collection included outstanding examples from Bugatti, Delage, Delahaye, Talbot, Voisin, Ferrari, Lancia, Alfa Romeo, Horch, Maybach, Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Lagonda, Jaguar, Aston Martin and Pegaso. Although he sold several cars during the 1980s and 1990s, he never parted with the Mercedes-Benz 500K Vanvooren, his personal favourite.

Following its purchase, Mr Strinati commissioned Carrosserie Roland Bodi to adjust the bonnet, repair the radiator, re-chrome the bumpers, repair the seats (likely referring to elements of the door panels, as the seats themselves appear completely original), and repaint the car in green—the colour it had when he first encountered it. The related quotation dated 25 February 1960 and the invoice for CHF 2,415 dated 26 April 1960 are on file. Strinati registered the Mercedes on 31 May 1960 under the number "GE 33961" and used it almost daily, often accompanied by his mother, who shared his deep affection for the car. In the 1970s, the 500K was taken out of service and placed into storage. In 1993, it was briefly exhibited at the Musée de l'Automobile Jean Tua in Geneva before being stored on axle stands in a purpose-built garage for the next 30 years.

In 2015, Martin Waltz—then researching a book on Vanvooren—wrote to Mr Strinati and inspected the 500K (documentation on file). More recently, he authored an article on the car in German, also on file.
A high-quality 1:43-scale collector's model of the car presented here is included in the sale. Released in 2014 by EMC/B&G in a limited edition of 150 examples, it is of outstanding quality—thanks in part to the support of Mr Strinati (correspondence on file).

This exceptional automobile, a unique fusion of German engineering and French design, is accompanied by an extensive archive of correspondence, period photographs, brochures, invoices and letters. Despite having been resprayed, in the 1960s, it remains in an outstanding state of originality and preservation, with the sumptuous green leather interior believed to be largely original. In recent years, the rarity, elegance and performance of these large, supercharged Mercedes models have made them among the most sought-after classic cars whenever they appear on the open market. This exceptionally well-documented example, hidden from public view for decades, is worthy of the closest inspection.

YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1931 DESCRIPTION:
• Original left-hand drive example
• Restored and re-bodied as a tourer in the 1970s
• Mentioned in John Webb de Campi's book, Rolls-Royce in America
• Present ownership since 2000

Chassis number '271-AJS' is one of approximately 100 built in the UK with left-hand drive. It is believed to be matching numbers, but this is as yet unconfirmed. Originally bodied in the USA by Huntington as a limousine, the Phantom was delivered new on 27th February 1932 to Mr C T Newberry of Irvington on Hudson, New York City. The car remained with the same family until 1971 when it returned to the UK for restoration and re-bodying by renowned coachbuilders FLM Panelcraft, as confirmed by stamps in the body panels. They named the bodywork 'Derby Tourer' after the Phantom I Derby Speedster, which was considered one of the finest bodies of its time (this car is mentioned in John Webb de Campi's book, Rolls-Royce in America).After restoration the Phantom returned to the USA where our vendor purchased it in 2000 from well known collector S Prestley Blake of Springfield, Massachusetts.

The vendor took the Rolls-Royce to his summer home in Cape Coral, Florida where it was used for rallies and concours events. In 2018 he decided to export the car to Sweden where it is currently registered for road use. The car is described as 100% correct mechanically, and according to the vendor is running well; it has not been driven much recently and would benefit from a repaint.

YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1923 DESCRIPTION:
• The most desirable, sporting Springfield Silver Ghost
• Original chassis, engine, and coachwork
• An older restoration
• Same family ownership since 2000
• Engine professionally rebuilt circa 2005
• Registered in Sweden

In December 1919 the newly created Rolls-Royce of America Incorporated purchased the American Wire Wheel Company's plant in Springfield, Massachusetts, from which the first US-built Silver Ghost emerged in January 1921. Unlike its British-built counterpart, the American 'Ghost could be ordered with 'factory' bodywork, usually by Brewster, the latter company being taken over by Rolls-Royce in December 1925. Right-hand drive remained the norm for US-built cars until early in 1925, the penultimate year of Silver Ghost production, when the switch was made to left-hand drive. The model was replaced by the New Phantom (retrospectively Phantom I) in 1926.

Prior to its acquisition of Brewster, Rolls-Royce of America Inc had set up the Rolls-Royce Custom Coach Works (RRCCW) program to organise the supply of 'factory' bodywork, commencing with the Silver Ghost and continuing on its New Phantom successor. Various established coachbuilders supplied bodies badged as 'RRCCW', including Massachusetts-based Merrimac, whose sporting Piccadilly Roadster was deservedly popular, some 70 being completed.

Retaining its original Piccadilly coachwork, this Springfield Silver Ghost was delivered new on 18th September 1923 to Mr Charles E F Clarke of 40 Wall Street. New York City. The car is finished in Old English White with beige leather interior, and is an early Springfield Ghost with right-hand drive and the four-speed gearbox (the model was only delivered in this configuration for the first two years). The car is believed to have been owned at one time by the well-known Campbell family in the USA. The current owner purchased the Rolls-Royce from S. Prestley Blake in the spring of year 2000 and it has been in their family's possession ever since.

The 'Ghost is an older restoration believed carried out in the 1970s-1980s. Around 2005 the engine underwent a comprehensive overhaul by renowned Rolls-Royce expert in Sweden, Kjell Lind, who has been helping the current owners with starting and running the car in recent years. The Ghost is today described as in good original condition. It is currently registered in Sweden and comes with Swedish registration documents, a folder of invoices, copies of the first US title, and other historic documents. As one would expect, this car is mentioned in the book Rolls Royce in America by John Webb de Campi.

Some ten years after the original's introduction it was felt that the time had come to update the Land Rover's somewhat primitive slab-sided styling. The result was the Series II, which featured more rounded sides. Introduced in 1958, the Series II was available with either the 2,286cc petrol engine or the newly developed 2,052cc diesel first seen in 1956 on what became known retrospectively as the 'Series I'. By this time the original permanent four-wheel drive freewheel transmission had been superseded by the more conventional selectable two- or four-wheel drive arrangement, with a set of low ratios available with the latter option selected. The chief development on the Series IIA was a much improved diesel engine.

This Series IIA 'Landie' was first registered on 22nd June 1966, and it is believed that Mr Strinati bought it new to use on his exploration and caving expeditions. Boasting the rare 'safari' roof, it was stored with all his speleological equipment in the rear, ready to embark on another tour. We believe that this car too is exceptionally original, most probably retaining its original paint. With its association with a world-renowned caving expert, this Land Rover is worthy of the closest inspection (unfortunately no folder has yet been discovered to further support the above). Again, recommissioning will be required prior to use and it should be noted that the aforementioned speleological equipment is not included in the sale.

auction_title: Scuderia Ferrari F1 – 1950 to 2019 - Over one hundred driver autographs – Collection of 136 models at 1/43 scale
description_block:
YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1950 DESCRIPTION:
An exceptional collection of 136 Ferrari Formula 1 models at 1/43 scale, each accompanied by a standing driver figure wearing full racing suit and helmet.
Each model originally derives from a high-quality kit, predominantly in white metal (such as BBR, Tameo, and others), and has been assembled by professional model makers.
Almost all models are accompanied by the autograph of the driver represented.
This collection traces the evolution of Scuderia Ferrari Formula 1 cars from 1950 to 2019.
Each car is presented with a plaque indicating the Grand Prix, model type, race number, and the signature of the model maker.
Beside each car stands its driver in full racing attire, with a separate plaque at his feet bearing his autograph.
The collection includes signatures from many legendary drivers, among them:
Fangio, Hawthorn, Hill, Ickx, Amon, Andretti, Lauda, Villeneuve, Prost, Barrichello, Massa, Alonso, Räikkönen, Schumacher, Irvine, Brooks, Mairesse, Vettel, Berger, Pironi, Regazzoni, and many others.
Also featured are autographs of drivers tragically killed during races:
Ascari (1955), Castellotti (1957), Collins (1958), Hawthorn (1959), von Trips (1961).
The ensemble represents an average of two models per year.
This lifetime collection was made possible only through privileged personal contact with the drivers and their representatives.
The majority of the autographs are executed in black felt-tip pen, applied to metal plaques protected by a transparent film.

The years 1969 and 1983 are not represented, as the kits available at the time were deemed insufficient in quality by the collector.
The collection is housed in two red display cabinets, supplied with the lot
(dimensions: 80 × 50 × 200 cm each).
